title: Science and Statistics
abstract: Aspects of scientific method are discussed: In particular, its representation as a motivated iteration in which, in succession, practice confronts theory, and theory, practice. Rapid progress requires sufficient flexibility to profit from such confrontations, and the ability to devise parsimonious but effective models, to worry selectively about model inadequacies and to employ mathematics skillfully but appropriately. The development of statistical methods at Rothamsted Experimental Station by Sir Ronald Fisher is used to illustrate these themes.

sections.summary: Scientific learning alternates between theory and practice through feedback from model failures. Flexibility, parsimony, selective concern for consequential errors, and appropriately applied mathematics make this iteration effective.

sections.summary: Fisher’s Rothamsted work illustrates how close engagement with real observations generates theory, from tea tasting and bacterial counts to extreme values and crop-yield trends. Orthogonal polynomials and residual checks show the interaction between fitting, criticism, and substantive explanations.

sections.summary: Rainfall–yield modeling illustrates parsimonious distributed lags, while potato trials motivate ANOVA, interactions, split-plot correction, and randomization. A simulation shows that error dependence can invalidate both parametric and rank tests unless randomization restores the needed protection.

sections.title: Designing investigations and redefining statistics
sections.summary: Analysis of inadequate trials pushed Fisher toward randomization, replication, blocking, factorial designs, and confounding. Adoption by practitioners supplied feedback and transformed statisticians from custodians of completed data into architects of investigations.

sections.summary: Opening the feedback loop leads either to unthinking routine analysis or mathematically elaborate work detached from scientific needs. Box argues for practical project experience in statistical training and presents Fisher’s integration of analysis, mathematics, and design as the model.
